etymologies.etymologyHTML: From astonish +‎ -ment.

definitions.definition: The feeling or experience of being astonished; great surprise.

quote.citation: 1630, John Milton, “On Shakespear” in Poems of Mr. John Milton, London: Ruth Raworth, 1645 p. 27,[1]
quote.text:
Thou in our wonder and astonishment
Hast built thy self a live-long Monument.

quote.citation: 1726 October 28, [Jonathan Swift], Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World.  […]  [Gulliver’s Travels], London:  […]  Benj[amin] Motte, […], →OCLC, (please specify |part=I to IV), page 98:
quote.text: […]  he dismissed all his Attendants with a turn of his Finger; at which, to my great astonishment, they vanished in an Instant, like Visions in a Dream, when we awake on a sudden.

quote.citation: 1811, [Jane Austen], chapter 1, in Sense and Sensibility […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London:  […]  C[harles] Roworth, […], and published by T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC, page 14:
quote.text: At these words, Marianne’s eyes expressed the astonishment, which her lips could not utter.

quote.citation: 1908, Lucy Maud Montgomery, chapter 3, in Anne of Green Gables‎[2], Boston: L.C. Page, page 41:
quote.text: Marilla’s astonishment could not have been greater if Matthew had expressed a predilection for standing on his head.

quote.citation: 2004, Andrea Levy, chapter 33, in Small Island‎[3], London: Review, page 330:
quote.text: Imagine my astonishment when, reaching the bustling street, every Englishwoman I look on is also attired in a dowdy housecoat.

quote.citation: 1905, Edith Wharton, The House of Mirth‎[4], New York: Scribner, Book 2, Chapter 9, p. 444:
quote.text: To find Ned Silverton among the habitual frequenters of Mrs. Hatch’s drawing-room was one of Lily’s first astonishments;

quote.citation: 1964, Roald Dahl, chapter 18, in Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Puffin, published 1998, page 83:
quote.text: Everything he had seen so far — the great chocolate river, the waterfall, the huge sucking pipes, the candy meadows, the Oompa-Loompas, the beautiful pink boat, and most of all, Mr. Willy Wonka himself — had been so astonishing that he began to wonder whether there could possibly be any more astonishments left.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Loss of physical sensation; inability to move a part of the body.

quote.citation: 1583, Philip Barrough, The Method of Phisicke‎[5], London: Thomas Vautroullier, Book 3, Chapter 37, p. 126:
quote.text: […]  there followeth astonishment of the leg that is neere, that it can neither be stretched out right, nor he cannot go on his feet.

quote.citation: 1601, C[aius] Plinius Secundus [i.e., Pliny the Elder], “[Book XXIX.] 5.”, in Philemon Holland, transl., The Historie of the World. Commonly Called, The Naturall Historie of C. Plinius Secundus. […], (please specify |tome=1 or 2), London:  […]  Adam Islip, →OCLC, page 363:
quote.text: […]  whosoever maketh water in the same place where a dog hath newly pissed, so as both vrines be mingled together, shall immediatly find a coldnesse and astonishment in his loines,

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Loss of mental faculties, inability to think or use one's senses.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalms 60:3:
quote.text: Thou hast shewed thy people hard things: thou hast made us to drink the wine of astonishment.

quote.citation: 1678, Aphra Behn, chapter 2, in The Lives of Sundry Notorious Villains‎[6], London: for the author, page 30:
quote.text: Upon the Stage he so charmed the people into astonishment with his babble, that he made them buy off amain his Drugs;

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Loss of composure or presence of mind.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto III”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, pages 35-36:
quote.text: […]  where of his cruell rageNigh dead with feare, and faint astonishment,Shee found them both in darkesome corner pent;

quote.citation: 1651, Thomas Hobbes, chapter 46, in Leviathan‎[7], London: Andrew Crooke, page 374:
quote.text: […]  as when a man ignorant of the Ceremonies of Court, comming into the presence of a greater Person than he is used to speak to, and stumbling at his entrance, to save himselfe from falling, lets slip his Cloake; to recover his Cloake, lets fall his Hat; and with one disorder after another, discovers his astonishment and rusticity.
